title: Typed positions are read as astropy reads them
claim: Degrees, letters, colons and spaces all give the position astropy gives, and nonsense is refused in plain words.
test: 28 strings, among them the challenge statement's own, were read by the page's parser and by astropy; 21 strings that are not positions must be refused.
pass_rule: Every position within 0.1 arcsec of astropy; every refusal has a plain message.

title: A star's catalogue position is moved to the date of a photo
claim: Proper motion, radial velocity and annual parallax move a catalogue position to the date of a photo as astropy moves it.
test: 10 stars (Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855-0714 and seven fast Gaia DR3 stars) on 4 dates between July 2025 and September 2026.
pass_rule: Every position within 0.01 pixel (0.0615 arcsec) of astropy.

title: JavaScript and Python give the same visits, pairs and stacks
claim: The visit rule, the match rule, the background, the co-add, the resampling and the difference are the same rule in both languages.
test: Shared vectors written by Python are read by JavaScript; a vector written by JavaScript is read by Python. Real stamps of an empty field and of Barnard's Star are among them.
pass_rule: Visits and pairs equal; numbers equal within 1e-6 relative.

title: Alignment from field stars finds a known shift
claim: Cross-correlating the stars of two photos of one field finds how far one is from the other.
test: Five real stamps were shifted by four known amounts between 0.1 and 0.7 pixel with a cubic spline (scipy), and the shift was measured again.
pass_rule: Every shift recovered within 0.05 pixel.

title: One source for every number, and the search of the literature
claim: Every number on the pages, in the project text and in the captions of the video is read from one file, every picture of a Checks row is the file that was reviewed, and what is known in the literature about the comet's carbon dioxide has been searched by hand and dated.
test: node tools/gate.mjs --check: a page that shows another number than numbers.json, a text of content/ that names a number that does not exist, a missing or changed picture of a row, and a PASS without a reviewer all fail it. The search of NASA ADS, the abstracts of the DPS 2026 meeting and of EPSC 2026, CBET and ATel is done by hand and written here with its date. Searched on 15 November 2026, by query (a person still reads it and signs it): NASA ADS (titles, abstracts and full text of 2025 and 2026, which hold the CBETs, ATels, MPECs, the COSPAR 2026 abstracts and the EPSC 2026 abstracts indexed by then), arXiv, and the EPSC 2026 programme. On C/2025 A6 they hold its discovery, orbit and brightness (2025CBET.5508....1F, 2025CBET.5594....1S, 2025CBET.5621....1G, 2025MPEC....D...55P), its jets (2025ATel17450....1S), optical spectra (2025ATel17456....1M), its OH seen by radio (2025ATel17463....1J, 2026RAA....26f1002J), its rotation (2026cosp...46..261T) and the polarisation of its tail (2026cosp...46..249W); nothing on its carbon dioxide. The abstracts of the DPS 2026 meeting were not in ADS and could not be opened without an account, so they were not searched.
pass_rule: The gate passes on the frozen tree; the search is dated and its sources are listed on this card; no text says that the comet's gas was found, measured or confirmed here before anyone else.
value: nothing on the comet’s carbon dioxide found on 15 November 2026; DPS 2026 not searched

title: A typed position, read straight from the archive: how long it takes and how it ends
claim: Any position on the sky gives two visits at one colour within seconds on a desktop link, or a plain message, and no error is left uncaught.
test: Chrome 157.0.8103.51 opened the viewer at 27 positions against the real archive, one after the other, each in a fresh window: the five test targets by name, both ecliptic poles and 20 random positions (seed 20261114). Times count from opening the page; megabytes are counted from the answers of the archive. The photos of each plan are counted against the index, and the stars of the targets are compared with their catalogue motion in every photo. One target was opened again over slowed links (400 kbit/s: message "slow"; 1.6 Mbit/s: first pair after 16.1 s, the rest offered as "Load more (13 MB)").
pass_rule: Every position ends in pictures or in a message with a next step; the browser reports no uncaught error; the median time to the first pair is under 4 seconds; both poles say that their plan is capped; Barnard's Star and one more target lie within 1 pixel of their catalogue motion in every photo of both visits.
value: 27 of 27 positions end in pictures (27) or a message (0); 0 uncaught errors; first pair: median 3.3 s, worst 4.6 s; full set: median 11.0 s, worst 17.2 s; median 16.1 MB, most 21.6 MB; 3 targets within 1 px of their catalogue motion (Barnard's Star: worst 0.73 px); at 4 positions the page asked a second time for pairs the reader had held back
reference: 27 of 27 positions, 0 errors, median first pair under 4 s, 2 targets within 1 px

title: What is typed is read, and what goes wrong is said
claim: A position typed in any usual form opens where astropy puts it, an old catalogue position of a fast star moves to the star, and every way the archive can fail has its own message with a next step.
test: Through the viewer page in Chrome 157.0.8103.51: 29 typed positions compared with astropy; the challenge statement's position for WISE 0855-0714 and Barnard's Star's position in 2000; 21 texts that are not positions. With a stand-in archive behind the page (tests/e2e/i1-live.spec.mjs): the bucket blocked, HTTP 503, HTTP 403, offline, a failure in the middle of loading, a link of 400 kbit/s, a link that turns slow while the first pair loads, one pair that stalls on a quick link, a position with no photos, a part of the sky that is not listed, one visit only, a saturated star, an empty patch; and the names (this site's list, the name service, a name nobody knows).
pass_rule: Every typed position within 0.1 arcsec of astropy; both old positions move to their star and say so; every text that is not a position gets a message; every fault shows its own message and a next step.
value: 29 of 29 typed positions (worst 0.0017 arcsec); 2 of 2 old positions moved to their star; 21 of 21 other texts answered; 12 of 12 faults and 1 of 1 name tests show their message

title: Colour axis: two hydrogen lines in their right place
claim: Read with the sky-distortion terms off, the wavelength tables put the Paschen-beta and Brackett-alpha lines of the planetary nebula NGC 6543 at their known colours.
test: NGC 6543 in every photo of detector 2 within 0.11 µm of Paschen-beta and of detector 5 within 0.1 µm of Brackett-alpha (76 and 55 photos). Flux in a 3-pixel aperture, background from a ring of 8 to 13.5 pixels; a Gaussian on a straight line is fitted to flux against the wavelength the tables give at the nebula. Expected: the laboratory vacuum wavelength moved by the nebula's velocity of -66 km/s (source of the velocity to be cited before review).
pass_rule: The fitted centre lies within 5 nm of the expected Paschen-beta wavelength and within 15 nm of the expected Brackett-alpha wavelength.
plain: colour checked on two known lines

title: Colour axis: the other four detectors
claim: In detectors 1, 3, 4 and 6 no line of known colour is available to this tool, so the tables are only compared with IRSA's own science wavelength maps. The check rests on IRSA's code and calibration.
test: The tables against the CWAVE layer of IRSA's Spectral WCS product (version cal-swcs-v5-2026-191) at 10,000 random pixels of each detector.
pass_rule: Not a pass or fail test: the largest difference is reported.
plain: colour rests on IRSA's own maps

title: Comet Lemmon: brighter at the colour of carbon dioxide
claim: On 25 and 26 February 2026 the brightest photo of comet C/2025 A6 (Lemmon) inside the carbon-dioxide band (4.20 to 4.32 µm) was at least 5 times brighter than the photos taken at the nearest colours on either side of the band.
test: Detector 5 photographed the comet 16 times on the two nights, each time at another colour; 15 photos could be measured (a photo with too many flagged pixels in the aperture gives no flux). Flux in an aperture of 2 pixels (12.3 arcsec) radius at the position JPL Horizons gives for the comet seen from SPHEREx; background from a ring of 40 to 55 pixels. The fluxes are lower limits, because the comet's glow reaches the ring: round the comet at 4.266 µm the sky level falls from 0.70 MJy/sr at 15 to 25 pixels to 0.44 in the ring and 0.41 just beyond it, while at the same place in August 2025 it is level (0.35, 0.34 and 0.34). Contrast of a night = the brightest photo of that night inside the band, over the mean of the two photos nearest the band: 4.193 µm (26 February) below it and 4.384 µm (25 February) above it, so each night takes one neighbour from the other night. The error counts the noise of the pixels, the background, and the scatter of up to 20 empty apertures of the same colour in each photo. Checks: with a ring of 15 to 25 pixels the contrast is 16.7 and 10.2; with an aperture of 5 pixels 10.9 and 8.5; with every aperture shifted by up to 0.2 pixel it stays between 12.7 and 17.3, and between 9.0 and 11.3. With any one photo left out that is not a night's brightest, the lowest contrast is 6.7. With a night's brightest photo left out, the next brightest gives: 25 February 3.1; 26 February 8.1; on 25 February the other photo inside the band sits at its edge, so that night's figure rests on a single photo. In the photo at 4.119 µm a star of the Gaia catalogue (G magnitude 12.8) lies 1.5 pixels from the comet and adds to its flux; that photo is not one of the three used.
pass_rule: The contrast is 5 or more on both nights.
plain: brighter at the colour of carbon dioxide on both nights

title: Comet Lemmon: the same sky without the comet
claim: For each of the 5 photos of the comet taken inside the band, a photo of August 2025 at the same colour shows nothing at the comet's place: the brightness belongs to the comet, not to that patch of sky.
test: For each of the 5 photos inside the band, the August 2025 photos of detector 5 that hold the same place were matched against it by the site's match rule (same detector, closest colour at that place, within half a bandwidth); the chosen templates differ in colour by 1.4 to 12.4 nm. Same aperture (2 pixels) and ring (40 to 55 pixels) at the same sky position. Template fluxes: -0.1, +1.5, +0.3, +0.5, +0.7 mJy against 162.5, 52.7, 136.2, 263.2, 71.7 mJy for the comet. Standard errors include the scatter of empty apertures of the same colour in both photos, which in this crowded field is far larger than the noise of the pixels (with the noise of the pixels and of the background alone, the smallest excess is 112 standard errors). The comet's two brightest positions are 52.2 arcmin and 37.5 hours apart, and the centre of its light lies 0.4 and 0.2 pixels from the JPL Horizons position.
pass_rule: Every template flux is under 5% of the comet's flux at that place, and every photo inside the band other than a night's brightest exceeds its template by 5 standard errors or more.
plain: nothing there in August 2025 at the same colour
value: largest template 2.9% of its comet flux; smallest excess 5.3 standard errors

title: Comet Lemmon: an earlier figure, corrected
claim: An earlier version of this analysis said the comet's excess inside the band was 88 times the scatter of empty sky. Measured on enough empty sky it is 4.7 times.
test: The earlier figure divided the excess by the scatter of the same estimate on 8 tracks of empty apertures, which happened to miss the stars of the field. On 128 empty tracks, some of which cross stars, the scatter is larger and the same excess is 4.7 times it. Both figures were measured on 14 November 2026 with an earlier estimate of the excess; this job does not compute them again, and the site quotes neither: it quotes the contrast of row K2.
pass_rule: Not a pass or fail test: a correction kept on record.
unit: times the scatter of empty tracks

title: Three moving targets land where their catalogues say
claim: From the image the WISE telescope took in 2010 to SPHEREx's latest visit, Epsilon Indi B, Barnard's Star and WISE 0855-0714 moved across the sky by the amount their catalogue astrometry gives.
test: The 2010 position is the centre of a Gaussian fitted in the AllWISE Atlas image of band W2 (for a star that saturates WISE, the centroid of the wings of its image); the SPHEREx position is the mean over the photos of the latest deep visit of detector 6 (the two stars) or the centre in the co-add of that visit (WISE 0855, too faint for one photo; a Gaia star beside it is fitted with it). The catalogue position is Gaia DR3 for the two stars and the astrometry of Kirkpatrick et al. 2021 as served by SIMBAD for WISE 0855 (not in Gaia; the paper itself was not opened), moved to each date with proper motion and parallax. Position only: no brightness is produced for Barnard's Star or WISE 0855. Beside WISE 0855-0714 lies the star Gaia DR3 5756956644387831296 (G 16.3), 4.3 arcsec from it at the date of the SPHEREx visit; it does not move and is fitted together with the target. In the 2010 image the target was 131 arcsec away, and what that image shows at the star's place lies 0.23 arcsec (0.04 of a SPHEREx pixel) from the star's Gaia position at that date (rule of the review: within 1 pixel).
pass_rule: Each measured shift differs from the catalogue shift by at most the tolerance in site/data/targets/tolerances.json (written before the jobs measured: half a SPHEREx pixel, plus half of what the object moved while the 2010 image was taken, plus one WISE beam for a star that saturates WISE), and each SPHEREx position lies within half a pixel of the catalogue position at that date. A fixed star beside a target is seen in the 2010 image within one SPHEREx pixel of its Gaia position. Barnard's Star saturates WISE: the core of its 2010 image is spoiled, and a Gaussian fitted there lands 6.4 arcsec from the catalogue, on the brighter side of the core. That value is not used. Its 2010 centre is the centroid of the wings of its image (2 to 4 beam widths out, started from the fit and repeated until it settles), 0.3 arcsec from the catalogue. The WISE beam in its tolerance (6.4 arcsec) was set when only the first value was known; without it the tolerance would be 5.8 arcsec and the difference of 0.1 arcsec would be within it all the same.
value: Epsilon Indi B 0.5 arcsec (0.14 px in SPHEREx alone); Barnard's Star 0.1 arcsec (0.04 px in SPHEREx alone); WISE 0855-0714 0.7 arcsec (0.07 px in SPHEREx alone)
unit: difference between measured and catalogue shift
reference: Epsilon Indi B 73.9 arcsec in 15.8 years; Barnard's Star 163.8 arcsec in 15.8 years; WISE 0855-0714 128.6 arcsec in 15.7 years
tolerance: Epsilon Indi B 4.2 arcsec; Barnard's Star 12.2 arcsec; WISE 0855-0714 4.8 arcsec; 0.5 px in SPHEREx alone

title: Motion within SPHEREx's own year
claim: Between two SPHEREx visits months apart, Epsilon Indi B and WISE 0855-0714 are seen to move, by the amount their catalogue astrometry gives with parallax included.
test: Detector 6. Epsilon Indi B: its position in every photo, averaged over each visit; first against last deep visit. WISE 0855: its position in the co-add of each of two visits (at each pixel the mean of the photos that may be used there; a Gaia star beside it is fitted with it); May 2025 is left out. It is measured a second time from only the photos with no unusable pixel round the target. Field stars measured the same way in the same photos are the control; the scatter of their shifts is added to the target's error.
pass_rule: Per target: the measured shift is at least 3 times its error from zero, and its east and north components are each within 3 times their error of the catalogue shift. The rule is applied with the robust scatter of the field stars in the error (the value given) and again with their plain standard deviation, and for WISE 0855 with both choices of photos; a target is shown only if it holds every way. A target that does not meet the rule gets its measured shift and error stated, and no motion view.
plain: motion seen within SPHEREx's own year
value: Epsilon Indi B 4.78 +- 0.15 arcsec; WISE 0855-0714 3.15 +- 0.83 arcsec
reference: Epsilon Indi B 4.66 arcsec; WISE 0855-0714 4.57 arcsec

title: RW Aurigae: its change per colour, with the saturated centre left out
claim: Between September 2025 and February to March 2026 RW Aurigae changed by a different amount in each colour band; a band is shown only where the change does not rest on pixels close to saturation.
test: Per detector, every one-to-one pair of frames the match rule accepts between the two visits. Three ways: all pairs (aperture of 3 pixels, every pixel); a common mask (in both frames everything within the radius that holds every flagged pixel of either aperture is left out, and the flux is that of the ring from there to 4.5 pixels); clean pairs (no flagged pixel in either aperture). Twenty comparison stars in the same frames are measured the same way, with the mask radius of the RW Aurigae pair nearest in colour. No data of other observers are used.
pass_rule: Per band: the sign of the change is the same with the common mask as with all pairs, and the comparison stars of that band, with the same mask, have a median ratio within 1% of 1. A band that fails reads "too bright to measure reliably".
value: D1 +18.8% (13 pairs) not shown; D2 +36.0% (11 pairs); D3 +28.2% (14 pairs); D4 not measurable; D5 -28.1% (7 pairs) not shown; D6 -37.6% (8 pairs) not shown
unit: change with the common mask, per detector

title: R Draconis is too bright to measure
claim: R Draconis is saturated in every SPHEREx photo of this release that holds it, so the tool gives no brightness for it.
test: Every photo that holds the star, in all six detectors, from 2025-05-16 to 2026-05-13: the flags of the pixels within 3 pixels of the star's position.
pass_rule: A photo is saturated when at least one of those pixels carries the flag OVERFLOW, NONLINEAR or BLOOM. The verdict "too bright to measure" stands if every photo checked is saturated.

title: A plain blink makes steady stars seem to change
claim: Flipping through SPHEREx photos that were taken at different colours makes steady stars seem to change in brightness; between photos of the same colour they hold.
test: Twenty steady comparison stars in the frames of RW Aurigae. The swing of a star is its brightest flux over its faintest (aperture of 3 pixels) among the photos flipped through: every photo of the first visit in time order (112 photos, six detectors); the photos of detector 1 in that visit; the two photos of a pair matched at the same colour in detector 1 (median over the star's pairs). The value is the median over the stars; RW Aurigae's own swing is given beside it.
pass_rule: The median swing of the comparison stars between matched photos is below 1.10, and below their swing at the other two stops.
plain: steady stars hold once the colour is matched
unit: median swing of the comparison stars
reference: RW Aurigae itself: x 49.7, x 2.71, x 1.24

title: Difference view and flipbook: do they show real change and nothing else?
claim: A difference of two visits taken at the same colour shows no change where there is none: an empty field averages to zero, and an injected source comes back at its true strength. Whether steady stars cancel is part of the same test, and the row says what it found.
test: 20 empty positions (no Gaia DR3 star brighter than G = 13 within 5 arcmin), each in two detectors, the ten of the earlier background test among them; the 20 steady comparison stars of RW Aurigae; 10 injected point sources (round Gaussian, sigma 1 pixel). Two views are judged apart: the difference of the co-adds of the two visits (at most 8 matched pairs) and each photo minus its same-colour twin (the flipbook). All built with the shared rules (visits, match, stack) on one 64 by 64 grid of 6.15 arcsec pixels. The mean is taken over the pixels with no flag but FULLSAMPLE; standard errors count pixels as independent.
pass_rule: Mean of an empty difference within 3 standard errors at 18 or more of 20 positions; 18 or more of 20 stars with no dark-bright pair above 3 noise units within 3 pixels; injected sources within 20% (10 of 10). A view is built at typed positions only if all three hold. Written before any measurement (pipeline/frozen/pb6_rule.json; the code in the column of the commit is the first 40 characters of the SHA-256 of that file, the commit itself is made by the person who commits).
plain: difference view tested on empty sky and on steady stars
value: empty 6/3 of 20 (with the 5-sigma clip of the earlier test, for comparison: 10/9), stars 0/0 of 20, injected 9/9 of 10 (co-adds/flipbook)

title: What the difference view can and cannot see
claim: A moving object shows as a dark-bright pair in the difference of two visits only when it moves far enough and is bright enough. The table says where that starts, for each of the six detectors; what is not in it is not seen.
test: Synthetic movers (round Gaussian, sigma 1 pixel) injected into the real matched co-adds, and into real single pairs, at 3 fixed positions of each detector, 8 injections per position for each of 8 speeds and 21 fluxes. The shift between visits is the speed times the time between them (median 181 days).
pass_rule: A mover shows when its dark-bright pair reaches 5 noise units in at least 80% of the injections. Rule written before the run (pipeline/frozen/limits_rule.json; the code in the column of the commit is the first 40 characters of the SHA-256 of that file). The table is shown whatever it says.
plain: what the tool can and cannot see
value: co-add: flux needed (median of the detectors) 13.9 mJy at 1.0 arcsec a year, 1.39 mJy at 10.0 arcsec a year, 0.781 mJy at 100.0 arcsec a year; the view shows 79% of its pixels; single pair: flux needed (median of the detectors) 31.6 mJy at 1.0 arcsec a year, 3.16 mJy at 10.0 arcsec a year, 1.39 mJy at 100.0 arcsec a year; the view shows 71% of its pixels

title: Agrees with a published ratio only within a wide margin, on the same photos (not independent)
claim: Interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS gave off more carbon dioxide in December 2025 than in August 2025. From the same SPHEREx photos, the December over August ratio of the band at 4.26 µm, corrected for distance, comes out as the published ratio within the combined error.
test: Flux of the comet in a 2-pixel aperture (12.3 arcsec) with a background ring of 40 to 55 pixels, in the photos of detector 5 (27 in August, 17 in December), the aperture centred on the position in IRSA's table of the comet's observations; 6 and 3 of the photos lie inside 4.20 to 4.32 µm. For each pass, a Gaussian is fitted to the flux above the continuum between 4.15 and 4.40 µm, and its area is the band. A band with hard edges is not used: moving its edges by 0.01 µm swings the ratio from 1.25 to 3.04. Scaling: the flux F in a fixed angle on the sky is proportional to Q / (r_h² x Δ), where Q is the number of molecules the nucleus gives off each second, r_h the distance from the Sun and Δ the distance from the telescope (gas leaving at a constant speed); so each photo is multiplied by r_h² x Δ before the fit. The published ratio is 3.0e27 over 1.6e27 molecules a second (Lisse et al.): a ratio of two production rates that those papers derive from their own model of the coma. The pages on disk do not say how, so this test cannot say whether the two quantities are the same; they are the same kind of quantity (carbon dioxide in a 2-pixel aperture on the same photos) and both are scaled to the same distances. With the scaling Δ² in place of Δ the ratio would be 1.47, outside the combined error of the published ratio. The ratio also depends on where the aperture sits: centred on the position from JPL Horizons as seen from SPHEREx (0.3 to 3 arcsec from IRSA's) it is 2.44 ± 0.09, which would not pass; centred on the light of each bright photo it is 2.41 ± 0.10; with a 5-pixel aperture, which hardly depends on the centring, it is 2.45 ± 0.13, which would not pass. In spring 2026 the band is not there: 3 photos in the band give +0.2 ± 1.0 mJy (3-sigma limit 3.2 mJy) against 18 mJy expected if production had stayed what it was in December; that is excluded at 18 sigma.
pass_rule: PASS if the ratio lies within the combined error of the published ratio (1.88 ± 0.34): |2.18 - 1.88| <= 0.35. The test is weak: the photos are the same ones, a result 20% away would also pass, and the centring of the aperture moves the result by more than its stated error. For that last reason the row is read as a limit, not as a pass.
plain: reproduces a published ratio on the same photos (not independent)

title: Spectra of a brown dwarf pair, compared with IRSA's own tool
claim: The spectrum that this tool builds from single SPHEREx photos for Epsilon Indi B and for three steady stars matches the one from IRSA's Spectrophotometry Tool to within 10%; this has not been compared yet.
test: The spectrum of Epsilon Indi B (a pair of brown dwarfs) and of three steady, unsaturated stars within 4 arcmin of it, from 327 photos in 5 visits: flux in a 2-pixel aperture, sky from a ring of 6 to 10 pixels, one point per photo. Compared with IRSA's SPHEREx Spectrophotometry Tool at the same positions and the same visit. The tool is a web application that runs a job for each source (minutes to hours) and has no script interface, so the comparison has to be made by hand: positions, our values and the rule are in the review sheet. Until it is made, every spectrum is labelled "relative only". As a rough check of the shape, the three stars' fluxes at the 2MASS bands are 0.99 times their catalogue brightness (median over J, H, K and the three stars; not a calibration: the bands are wide). The aperture correction from the point-spread-function model is not applied: the scatter of the stars about their neighbours in colour is 3.5% with it and 3.3% without.
pass_rule: PASS if the median ratio of our fluxes to those of IRSA's tool, over the colours both have, lies between 0.9 and 1.1; otherwise the spectra stay labelled "relative only".
plain: spectra are relative only until compared with IRSA's tool

title: Pluto in plain photos, blinked against another visit
claim: In plain SPHEREx photos, with nothing subtracted, Pluto is a point of light where JPL Horizons says it should be, and that place is empty in a photo of the same colour taken at another visit.
test: The photos and their same-colour twins are those of row K-pluto: JPL Horizons gives Pluto's place as SPHEREx saw it at each photo's time, the frame index gives the photos that hold it, and the shared match rule gives each a twin from another visit in which Pluto is at least 12 pixels away. At most 24 pairs per detector, evenly spaced in time. In the photo, background removed and smoothed with a Gaussian of 1 pixel, the brightest pixel within 1.5 pixels of the predicted place is measured and a round Gaussian is fitted there; in the twin, resampled onto the photo's pixels and treated the same way, the brightest pixel within 1 pixel of that fit. Position only: no brightness, spectrum or ice is claimed.
pass_rule: In at least one detector at least 80 percent of the pairs show a light of at least 5 noise units whose fitted centre is within 1 pixel (6.15 arcsec) of the Horizons place, with nothing of 3 noise units or more there in the twin. The rule is in pipeline/frozen/pluto_blink_rule.json; it was written after the difference test of row K-pluto had failed and before any plain photo was measured for it.
value: detector 1: 14 of 24 pairs; best detector for the light alone: D3 23 of 24, its twins empty in 14

title: The index of photos, built again from the archive for one week
claim: One command builds the index of photos from the archive alone: the bucket's listing of a week and each photo's own header. For a whole week it gives the photos of the installed index, each in the same tiles. It does not give every row digit for digit: a row that the installed index took from the archive's image search, and not from the photo's header, can differ in its last digit.
test: Week 2025W46_1A, the one with the fewest photos of the 110 weeks in the installed index. The command listed the week in the archive's public bucket (9,169 photos), read from each photo the cards CRPIX1 to MJD-END of its header with one range request, and wrote rows and tiles into a folder of its own. The rows were read back from those tiles (9,169 photos) and compared with the rows of the same photos in the installed index (site/idx, 9,169 photos of that week): the photo (week, version, observation, exposure, detector), the mid-time as stored, to 0.000001 day, the four corners, and the tiles that hold the row. 9,169 rows compared, 608 differ; 0 photos are in one index only; 0 rows lie in other tiles. Reading the headers took 37 s for a thousand photos (9,169 photos, the listing included, six requests at a time). Of the rows that differ, 598 differ in the mid-time, by up to 0.000001 day, and 14 in a corner, by up to 0.0001 degree. The installed index took 408,078 of its rows from the archive's image search and not from the headers (meta.json, sources). The search gives the start and the end of an exposure to 0.000001 day, and their mean can fall one digit beside the mid-time that the header itself gives (MJD-AVG). Built from the same header with the times rounded that way and the corners rounded once, 608 of the 608 rows are the installed rows digit for digit; 0 are not explained.
pass_rule: PASS if the week has the same photos in both, every row in the same tiles, and no row differs: mid-times equal as stored, corners within 0.000001 degree. A limit, not a pass, if the photos and the tiles are the same and every row that differs is the installed row digit for digit once the header's times are rounded as the archive's image search rounds them. FAIL otherwise.
plain: one week built again from the archive: the same photos, a last digit apart in some rows

title: A gallery of fast stars and "Can you spot it?": not built
claim: Enough fast stars and matched empty fields exist for a fair spot-the-mover set.
test: Gaia DR3 stars moving more than 1 arcsec a year with two visits, each compared with its catalogue position in a 2010 AllWISE image and in SPHEREx; six empty fields of matched star density sought for the set.
pass_rule: At least 8 stars on their catalogue position within 1 pixel and not saturated in any photo used, with 6 matched empty fields. Otherwise neither the gallery nor the set is built.
value: 24 of 24 tested stars on their position; the set could not be completed (4 of 6 movers, too few empty fields)

title: Pluto, photo by photo: not shown
claim: Pluto is found where JPL Horizons predicts it in the difference of same-colour photos.
test: 214 photos that hold Pluto; each photo minus its same-colour twin from the other visit; the brightest residual within 10 pixels compared with the predicted position, detector by detector.
pass_rule: Found within 1 pixel of the prediction in at least 80% of the difference photos of one detector. Otherwise Pluto is not shown.
